article.title: An AI Agent Should Have Its Own Identity
article.author: OpenAI learning editor

paragraphs.en:
Organizations already manage identities for employees, applications, and machines. AI agents add a new question: when an autonomous system takes an action, whose identity should the system record? If every agent uses the same shared service account, it can become difficult to understand which agent acted, which human or workflow authorized it, and what permissions were appropriate at that moment.

Giving an agent a distinct identity does not mean treating it exactly like a person. It means creating a technical identity that can be authenticated, authorized, logged, and revoked. When an agent calls a database or API, the receiving system can recognize the agent rather than seeing only a generic credential shared by many processes.

Identity is closely connected to authorization. An agent may act on behalf of a human user, a team, or an automated business process. The system needs to know both who the agent is and what authority has been delegated to it. For example, an assistant may be allowed to read a user's calendar and draft a meeting request but not send an invitation to external participants without approval.

Delegation should have scope. A user who can access thousands of customer records may ask an agent to work on only one account. It does not follow that the agent should automatically inherit every permission the user has. The delegated authority can be limited by resource, action, time, or transaction value. This is another application of least privilege.

Separate identity also improves auditing. Imagine that three agents use the same credential and one of them changes a record incorrectly. A log showing only the shared account does not tell investigators which workflow caused the change. If each agent has a distinct identity and each action records the initiating user or process, the organization can reconstruct the chain more accurately.

Identity becomes even more important when agents communicate with other agents. Agent A may delegate a task to Agent B, which then calls a third-party service. The organization needs a way to preserve the chain of authority. Otherwise, a downstream service may see a valid request without knowing whether the original user actually authorized that type of action.

Credentials should also be short-lived where possible. An agent performing a temporary task may receive a token that expires after the workflow ends. If the agent is compromised or behaves unexpectedly, administrators should be able to revoke its access without disabling unrelated systems. Shared, permanent credentials make this much harder.

There are practical challenges. Organizations need naming rules, lifecycle management, monitoring, and policies for thousands or potentially millions of agent instances. Some agents are temporary; others are long-running. The identity system must distinguish the stable agent or application from an individual execution session.

The design principle is simple even if implementation is not: actions should be attributable. A secure agent architecture should make it possible to answer, 'Which agent did this? Who or what authorized it? What permission was used? When did that permission expire?' Better prompts cannot answer those infrastructure questions. Identity, authorization, delegation, and logging must work together.

paragraphs.ja: AI Agentが実際の操作を行う場合、applicationやmachineと同様に識別可能なtechnical identityが必要です。複数Agentが同じservice accountを共有すると、どのAgentが、誰のauthorityで、どのpermissionを使ったか分かりにくくなります。Agent identityはauthentication、authorization、logging、revocationが可能であるべきです。人間が広い権限を持っていてもAgentへ全権限を自動継承させず、resource、action、time、transaction valueでdelegationを限定します。複数Agent間の委任ではauthority chainを残す必要があります。credentialは短期間にし、異常時に個別revocationできる設計が重要です。

quiz.question: Why is a shared service account weak for agents?
quiz.answer: It makes attribution and permission control difficult.
